_comment: Which books are paid. This file is the single source of truth.
index_json.py stamps each row of data/index.json with `paid`, so the client
can draw a lock without asking anything; split_content.py uses the same list
to decide which book files leave the published site; upload_content.py pushes
those files into Supabase, where a row-level policy decides who may read them.
A book missing from `paid` is free — that is the default, and a fork that
never touches Supabase gets every book free with no code change.
Moving a book between free and paid is an edit here plus:
python3 site/tools/index_json.py       # restamp the index
python3 site/tools/split_content.py    # move the file
python3 site/tools/upload_content.py   # push it to Supabase
Nobody's subscription has to change: a subscription is to the app, not to a
list of books.
_free: Six free books, and they are the ones a beginner starts with. The funnel is:
learn on the free shelf, pay when the level you need is behind a lock.
The first five carry a learner from A1 to B1, which is where most people who
ielts-19 is free for a different reason: it is the sample. Somebody deciding
whether to buy needs to work a whole IELTS test, not read about one, and one
of three tests given away is the cheapest way to show what the other two are.
The exam shelf is where the money is, so the free taste belongs there too.

_comment: How many units of each paid book are given away as a free sample.
build_samples.py writes site/data/sample/<id>.json with that many units,
and the app opens a locked book onto them instead of a bare lock screen.
This is a pricing decision, not a technical one. Two units of a grammar
book is a spread and a half — enough to work, not enough to learn from.
An IELTS unit is a whole forty-question test section, so those give one,
and ielts-19 is already free in its entirety as the exam-shelf sample.
0 means no sample at all: the book keeps the plain lock screen.
